clinical_targets.goal: Complete alleviation of primary presenting complaint and systemic stability
Return of baseline physiological parameters (vital signs, CBC, metabolic panel)
Full return to activities of daily living (ADLs) and functional autonomy

steps_summary: Step 1: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
Step 2: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)

steps.title: Step 1: First-Line Therapy: Conservative Foundation & Targeted Monotherapy
steps.rationale: Initial management of Diagnostic Imaging focuses on non-pharmacological foundations, patient education, elimination of precipitating triggers, and initiating evidence-based first-line monotherapy. Treatment should begin at the lowest effective dose with periodic reassessment.

drug_classes.role: Standard initial therapy for mild-to-moderate Diagnostic Imaging.
drug_classes.dosing: Initiate standard therapeutic dosing; titrate over 2–4 weeks based on clinical response and tolerability.
drug_classes.pearls: Monitor for early therapeutic response; assess patient compliance and verify baseline organ function.

steps.title: Step 2: Second-Line / Dual Add-On Therapy (Inadequate Response to Step 1)
steps.rationale: For patients with persistent symptoms, partial response, or disease progression after 4–8 weeks of Step 1 therapy, escalate by titrating to the maximum tolerated dose or adding a complementary second-line agent with a distinct mechanism of action.

drug_classes.role: Adjunctive or alternative therapy for treatment escalation in Diagnostic Imaging.
drug_classes.dosing: Introduce second-line agent as add-on dual therapy or sequential switch; reassess at 4–6 weeks.
drug_classes.pearls: Screen for drug-drug interactions and additive adverse effects before combining systemic agents.

steps.title: Step 3: Third-Line / Advanced Specialty Therapy & Multidisciplinary Escalation
steps.rationale: Patients with severe, recalcitrant, or treatment-refractory Diagnostic Imaging require multidisciplinary subspecialist evaluation and consideration of advanced therapies (biologics, targeted small molecules, immunosuppressive regimens, or specialized combination protocols).

drug_classes.role: Targeted intervention for severe or refractory Diagnostic Imaging.
drug_classes.dosing: Specialist-guided dosing with pre-treatment laboratory clearance and structured monitoring.
drug_classes.pearls: Perform required baseline screening (e.g. latent infections, CBC, organ function panels) prior to initiation.

steps.title: Step 4: Refractory / Salvage Protocols & Interventional / Inpatient Care
steps.rationale: Reserved for treatment-resistant, acute progressive, or complicated disease. Protocol includes parenteral salvage therapies, procedural or surgical interventions, inpatient stabilization, and long-term rehabilitation.

drug_classes.role: Rescue intervention for complicated or refractory Diagnostic Imaging.
drug_classes.dosing: Hospital or tertiary center procedural protocol.
drug_classes.pearls: Careful risk-benefit assessment by a multidisciplinary clinical care team.

special_populations.renal_impairment: Calculate CrCl using Cockcroft-Gault before prescribing narrow therapeutic index drugs.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: Review patient's complete prescription and OTC medication list for drug-induced liver injury (DILI).
special_populations.pregnancy_lactation: Verify safety in pregnancy and lactation databases before prescribing any new therapeutic class.
special_populations.elderly: Perform medication reconciliation to eliminate unnecessary polypharmacy and anticholinergic load.

style_3_monograph.summary: What is diagnostic imaging? Diagnostic imaging refers to medical tests that create pictures of the inside of the body. These pictures help your health care provider see your organs, bones, blood vessels, and tissues. Imaging tests can help find the cause of symptoms, detect disease early, monitor an illness or injury, and guide treatment. What are different types of diagnostic imaging? Different machines are used to create pictures inside your body. The type of imaging your provider uses depends on your symptoms and the part of your body being checked. Common types of diagnostic imaging include: X-rays CT (computed tomography) scans Nuclear medicine scans MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) scans Ultrasound Why is diagnostic imaging done? Diagnostic imaging tests help providers understand health problems and make decisions about care. These tests may be used to: Find health problems early Learn what causes pain or other symptoms Plan treatment Monitor a condition or see how well treatment is working Some imaging tests can also help guide medical procedures, such as placing catheters, stents, or other medical devices inside the body. How is diagnostic imaging done? Each diagnostic imaging test is different, but many follow similar steps. During an imaging test: Some tests require you to change clothes or remove metal items, such as jewelry or glasses Some tests require you to fast (not eat or drink) or drink contrast material (a substance that helps some parts of your body show up more clearly on the images) Many imaging tests take only a short time Some tests require you to stay still inside an imaging machine, which may feel uncomfortable Some tests use a small amount of radiation Always tell your provider if you are pregnant or think you may be pregnant. After most imaging tests, you can return to normal activities right away. A specialist called a radiologist reviews the images and shares the results with your provider.
style_3_monograph.treatment: Consult healthcare provider for individualized management.
